Description: Bronze prutahs struck at the Jerusalem mint for Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judaea AD 26-36 under the emperor Tiberius. Two types were issued: year 16 (AD 29) with three bound ears of barley and the inscription 'Julia Caesar' on the obverse and a simpulum (libation ladle) with 'Tiberius Caesar' on the reverse; and years 17-18 (AD 30-31) with a lituus (augur's wand) on the obverse and the date in a wreath on the reverse, including dies with the blundered 'HZ' for 'LIZ'. Pilate's own name does not appear on the coins; they are attributed to his prefecture by mint, dates, and types.
Interpretations: Securely attests Pilate's prefecture and its dates alongside the Pilate Stone inscription. The exclusively Roman cultic symbols (simpulum, lituus) on coinage circulating in a largely Jewish and Samaritan province show Pilate promoting Roman religion, consistent with the Gospel portrait of a governor insensitive to Jewish feeling. Nuance to state plainly: Pilate's name is absent from the coins — the attribution rests on the prefecture's minting, not a personal inscription.
BiblicalSignificance: Luke 3:1 dates John the Baptist's ministry to the governorship of Pontius Pilate in Judaea; these coins are the everyday currency of that governorship, struck in the very years of Jesus' ministry.
CurrentLocation: Examples in the British Museum and the Israel Museum
